output.title: What contact decay hides in a small business
output.body:
Contact decay is not usually a big strategy problem. In a 1–10 person business, it is the quiet point where a lead, customer, or supplier contact goes stale and nobody notices until the chance to follow up is already gone. That can happen in a CRM, an inbox, or a spreadsheet with neat columns and no real follow-through. The issue is visibility: if you do not know which contacts have gone quiet, you cannot tell whether you have a sales problem, a process problem, or just a memory problem. Human memory is a brave little filing system, but it is not a system.

The practical decision is simple: before you build any automation, check whether contact decay is actually visible in your current workflow. Take one week of your contact list and mark the records you know have gone dormant. Then write down how you noticed each one. Was it a missed reply, an old quote, a customer who never came back, or a note you found too late?

If the contacts already live in digital tools and the quiet ones are easy to spot once you look, a lightweight flag may be worth building. If most contacts arrive by phone call or walk-in, AI may not be the right fit. Once you see which contacts have gone quiet and why, you will know whether a system to flag them is worth building.
